$comment: Cross-runtime golden vectors for Ion's `decimal` primitive (exact-precision decimal).

wireFormat.container: CBOR tag 4 (decimal fraction, RFC 8949 §3.4.4) wrapping a definite-length 2-element array [exponent, mantissa].
wireFormat.exponent: A plain CBOR integer (major type 0 or 1), minimal-length. Always fits i32.
wireFormat.mantissa: A plain CBOR integer (major type 0/1) when the value fits the i64/u64 range, otherwise a tag 2 (positive) or tag 3 (negative) bignum whose byte string is the MINIMAL-length big-endian magnitude. For tag 3 the magnitude is -1 - value, per RFC 8949.
wireFormat.readerLeniency: Readers accept an indefinite-length inner array, a non-normalised mantissa, and a bignum that would have fitted a plain int. They reject any other tag, an arity other than 2, and a non-array payload — with a TYPED decode error.

canonicalForm.rule: The mantissa is NORMALISED on write: trailing decimal zeros are stripped and the exponent raised to compensate. Zero is always [0, 0].
canonicalForm.why: 1.50 and 1.5 are the same number. Without a canonical form a C# `1.50m` (which remembers its scale: unscaled 150, scale 2) and a TypeScript `IonDecimal(-1, 15n)` would compare equal but serialise to different bytes, breaking the byte-identity rule the same way shortest-form floats did.
canonicalForm.chosenOverAlternative: The alternative — 'leave the mantissa as authored' — was rejected because C# decimal, JS bigint and a Rust i128 do not agree on what 'as authored' means: C# is the only one of the three that carries a trailing-zero scale at all, so it alone could ever produce the un-normalised form.
canonicalForm.negativeZero: C# decimal can hold a negative zero (`-0.0m`). It normalises to mantissa 0, and CBOR has no negative zero integer, so -0.0m and 0m are the same four bytes. Documented, not accidental.

types.cs: System.Decimal. Its range (|v| <= 2^96-1 unscaled, scale 0..28) is NARROWER than tag 4 allows, so out-of-range decoding is a typed error — see `inCSharpDecimalRange`.
types.ts: IonDecimal { exponent: number, mantissa: bigint } — dependency-free, and deliberately NOT `number`, which is binary floating point and cannot hold an exact decimal.
types.rust: ion_rustcore::IonDecimal { exponent: i32, mantissa: i128 } — dependency-free, no rust_decimal. A mantissa outside i128 is a typed decode error.

howToConsume: encode: build the value from `exponent` and `mantissa` (the AUTHORED, possibly non-canonical
pair) and expect exactly `hex`, which encodes `canonicalExponent`/`canonicalMantissa`.
decode: read `hex` and re-encode it, expect `hex` back.
C# only: skip the encode/decode round trip when `inCSharpDecimalRange` is false, and instead
assert that decoding `hex` raises the typed out-of-range error.
For each entry of `decodeOnly`: read `hex`, re-encode, expect `reencodedHex`.
For each entry of `malformed`: reading `hex` must raise the runtime's TYPED decode error.

vectors.name: zero
vectors.notes: Zero is canonically [0, 0]. Any authored zero (0.00, -0.0, 0E+5) normalises to these four bytes, so a C# decimal's negative zero and a positive zero are indistinguishable on the wire — CBOR has no negative zero integer.

vectors.name: zero-authored-scaled
vectors.notes: ENCODE-ONLY IN SPIRIT: authored as 0.00 (exponent -2), canonicalises to exponent 0. Same bytes as 'zero'.

vectors.name: one-point-five-zero
vectors.notes: CANONICAL-FORM GUARD. 1.50 and 1.5 are the same number, so they MUST be the same bytes. The mantissa is normalised by stripping trailing zeros — without this rule a C# `1.50m` (scale 2) and a TypeScript IonDecimal(-1, 15n) would disagree byte-wise while comparing equal.

vectors.name: hundred-from-scaled-mantissa
vectors.notes: Normalisation can drive the exponent POSITIVE: 1000 x 10^-1 -> 1 x 10^2.

vectors.name: positive-exponent
vectors.notes: A positive exponent is a plain unsigned CBOR int.

vectors.name: smallest-cs-scale
vectors.notes: Exponent -28 is the most negative a C# decimal can hold.

vectors.name: out-of-cs-range-exponent
vectors.notes: OUT-OF-RANGE GUARD. Exponent -30 exceeds C# decimal's maximum scale of 28. Decoding this in C# must produce a TYPED error, not an OverflowException and not a silently rounded value. TypeScript and Rust decode it exactly.

vectors.name: u64-mantissa
vectors.notes: ulong.MaxValue. Still a plain CBOR unsigned int (0x1b + 8 bytes), not a bignum — the mantissa only becomes a tag 2/3 bignum once it leaves the i64/u64 range.

vectors.name: i64-min-mantissa
vectors.notes: long.MinValue: the last mantissa that is still a plain CBOR negative int (0x3b + 8 bytes).

vectors.name: bignum-mantissa-positive
vectors.notes: 2^64, one past ulong.MaxValue: the first mantissa that must be written as a tag 2 bignum with a minimal-length big-endian magnitude.

vectors.name: cs-decimal-max
vectors.notes: decimal.MaxValue exactly (2^96 - 1). In range for C#, and a 12-byte tag 2 bignum on the wire.

vectors.name: out-of-cs-range-mantissa
vectors.notes: OUT-OF-RANGE GUARD. decimal.MaxValue + 1 (2^96). Off by exactly one from the previous vector, so it isolates the boundary check rather than the magnitude.

vectors.name: out-of-cs-range-mantissa-negative
vectors.notes: decimal.MinValue - 1, as a tag 3 negative bignum (magnitude = -1 - value = 2^96 - 1).

vectors.name: pi-28-digits
vectors.notes: 28 significant digits: the most a C# decimal can carry, and a bignum mantissa. In range.

vectors.name: negative-exponent-large-mantissa
vectors.notes: Bignum mantissa combined with a negative exponent.

decodeOnly.name: reads-non-canonical-trailing-zeros
decodeOnly.notes: LENIENCY. A peer that did not normalise still decodes; re-encoding canonicalises it. This is the read side of the 1.50 == 1.5 rule.

decodeOnly.name: reads-non-canonical-bignum-for-small-mantissa
decodeOnly.notes: LENIENCY. A tag 2 bignum holding a value that fits an int is accepted on read and re-encoded as a plain int.

decodeOnly.name: reads-indefinite-length-inner-array
decodeOnly.notes: LENIENCY. An indefinite-length inner array (0x9F ... 0xFF) is accepted. Writers always emit a definite length of 2.

decodeOnly.name: reads-zero-with-nonzero-exponent
decodeOnly.notes: 0 x 10^5 is zero; canonical zero is [0, 0].

malformed.name: wrong-tag
malformed.notes: Tag 5 is bigfloat (mantissa x 2^exponent), a different value for the same array. Rejected.

malformed.name: wrong-arity
malformed.notes: Tag 4 is defined as exactly two elements.
